title: Shishupala
hook: the angry kings gather around Shishupala, Bhishma speaks of a sleeping lion, and Bhima has to be held back

segments.voice: Yesterday Shishupala made his case and walked out, and Yudhishthira followed him with gentle words. One gentle sentence before a sharp one.

A room can turn in a few seconds. One person's anger becomes a murmur, the murmur becomes a group, and the group starts talking about a fight. That's where the Rajasuya is now. Other kings have gathered around Shishupala, and in the telling they begin to talk of war, of spoiling the rite before it's finished. Yudhishthira, the host, is worried, and he turns again to his grandfather. Two kinds of anger in one hall: the kind that spreads, and the kind that has to be held back.
screen: `ONE ANGER BECOMES A CROWD.` → `TALK OF WAR AT THE RITE.` → `THE HOST IS WORRIED.`

segments.voice: First, the youngest Pandava speaks up. Sahadeva, who carried the arghya to Krishna, dares anyone who objects to the honor to answer him. Nobody does. Then Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what to do about the kings. Bhishma isn't troubled. He gives an image instead of a plan: these kings are like dogs barking around a sleeping lion, and the lion hasn't woken up yet. A striking thing to say about a room full of crowned rulers. Shishupala turns his anger on Bhishma. He mocks the old man with a little fable about a bird that preaches caution while picking scraps of meat from a lion's teeth: that's Bhishma, all fine words and no courage. He mocks the stories told about Krishna's childhood, too. That's when Bhima rises. The poem describes his rage as terrible to see, his eyes blazing, ready to spring at Shishupala. And Bhishma, the very man being insulted, holds him back and calms him down. So look at the hall. Shishupala's anger keeps spreading, pulling in kings, reaching for anyone nearby. Bhima's is just as hot, but it's caught and held by an elder who takes the insult and refuses to let it become a brawl. And Krishna, the sleeping lion in Bhishma's picture, still hasn't moved.
screen: `SAHADEVA'S DARE.` · `DOGS AROUND A SLEEPING LION.` · `SHISHUPALA MOCKS BHISHMA.` · `BHISHMA HOLDS BHIMA BACK.` · then, large: `ANGER THAT SPREADS, ANGER THAT IS HELD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that made you angry recently, and let yourself feel a little of it: the heat, the quickening. Don't push it away; hold it the way a hand rests on a friend's shoulder, and breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in, a few times. If you pray, you can bring that anger into your prayer just as it is; if not, simply keep breathing with it.
Shishupala. The king whose anger spreads through the hall, who mocks Bhishma, and who stirs Bhima to a rage that Bhishma has to hold back.
Your line: one long breath out first. Held anger is still anger; it just isn't a brawl yet. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In some retellings of the Sabha Parva, Bhishma restraining Bhima, even while Shishupala mocks him, is told as a picture of an elder's self-control.

original.note: Sanskrit śiśupāla: the name of the king of Chedi, Krishna's cousin.

trapdoor: what you thought: one angry guest.
what it means: an anger that spreads to other kings and drives Bhima to rage, until Bhishma holds him back.
what a scholar hears: Bhishma's sleeping-lion image casts Krishna as the one who hasn't acted yet, so the delay itself becomes part of the story.
recall: the pale one, born of a mother's fear

chat.says: Bhishma got insulted to his face. Why did he stop Bhima from fighting?
options: He held the anger back so the insult wouldn't turn into a brawl at the rite.
He agreed with Shishupala's fable and felt he'd earned the insult.
He wanted to fight Shishupala himself and didn't want Bhima to go first.
chat.meaning: Bhishma, the one insulted, calmed Bhima and held him back. That anger was held; Shishupala's kept spreading.

Bhima.meaning: second Pandava brother, famed for strength and anger

Sahadeva.meaning: the youngest of the five Pandava brothers

arghya.meaning: a respectful welcome of water and gifts for an honored guest

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Sahadeva's challenge to objectors and that no one answered it (Ganguli also mentions flowers falling; omitted here).
Confirm Bhishma's image of dogs barking around a sleeping lion, said to Yudhishthira about the kings.
Confirm Shishupala's fable of the bird (named bhulinga in Ganguli) that urges caution while picking meat from a lion's teeth; the bird's name is left out here.
Confirm that Bhishma himself restrains the enraged Bhima.
